style: A sharp, warm product explainer for a business audience. Brisk and confident, clear diction, like a good documentary narrator who respects your time. Not salesy. Keep pauses short.
music: Minimal, warm instrumental underscore for a product explainer film. Soft pulsing synths, gentle felt piano, light clean percussion, about 92 BPM, steady and quietly optimistic, building slightly toward the end. No vocals. About two minutes.

lines.text: Every team using AI hits the same wall: it doesn't know how you like things done. Here's how everyday corrections become a skill that gets it right the first time.
A skill is saved instructions for one job. This one draws ASCII art. Every time someone uses it in Claude Code, the use lands on the Desk.
It draws thin outlines. This person wants solid, shaded drawings that stand on a shadow, so they say so, in plain words.
Each correction becomes a yes-or-no check. Is the body filled in? Is there a shadow?
When it's right, they accept it into the Lab. That's the benchmark: built from real work, not made-up tests.
A use that isn't worth learning from gets dismissed.
Then, Optimize. A teacher model reads what the skill gets wrong, and writes a new version.
Every version is run on every case, first try, with no one steering, and graded on the checks.
A version only replaces the skill if it passes more checks. Two does, barely. Then three. Then four: from sixteen of thirty-one, to twenty-six.
Most versions lose, and never ship. That's why skills need tests: so a worse version can't quietly replace a better one.
Back to work. Now the drawings come out right the first time. Nothing left to correct.
Every new case raises the bar: fifty checks, across ten cases.
Version eleven gets forty-six of the fifty. Of thirteen versions, five won and eight lost.
Corrections per drawing: from two, to zero. Steering is the data. Checks are the benchmark. Testing is the guardrail.
